chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter takes place in Grandmother's patchwork room. A quilt, a rug, table tops, a desk, grids, mats and square tiles are the shapes, and laying lace round them, covering them with tiles and counting squares shows what the perimeter and the area of a shape are, how they differ, and how to find them for rectangles and squares. A short video explains each idea, and an interactive tool lets the student try it alone.

points.title: Videos teach, tools explore
points.text: Every idea has one short concept video. The tool that follows is where the student explores, builds and checks the idea alone, with hints, retry and reset. Six tools, each with its own purpose, follow the chapter's own plan.

points.title: A tool in three steps
points.text: Each tool opens with a short recall of the video idea, then lets the student play and apply it, and ends with the chapter's own question, used exactly as the book gives it.

points.title: Every book question has its own video
points.text: Every solved example, Let Us Do and Let Us Explore question and every answerable prompt of the book is its own short video with a step by step solution and a question picture and a solution picture, in a Questions topic that follows the idea it practises.

points.title: The picture is the mathematics
points.text: Quilts, tables, grids and rectangles of patches carry each idea: the border outlined for perimeter, the squares inside counted for area, with every edge and every square clear.

points.title: Only the book's numbers
points.text: The quilt, the tables, the desk, the grids, the mats and every question are the book's own. Any number the plan adds is a practice value and is said to be one.

tool_config.title: Quilt Lace
tool_config.idea: Find out by laying lace along the border of a quilt that the lace needed is the length all the way round, counted in units: the red and blue reels run out, the green reel fits exactly, and two laces of different colours can share the border. This is the free first try of the chapter, so it asks and shows; the video that follows names the perimeter.
tool_config.screen: Grandmother's sunny patchwork room, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. The quilt cover is spread on the floor and is the largest thing on screen: 15 patches along the long side and 10 patches along the short side in rows of green, red and yellow patches with a pink rim, as in your maths book. Every patch side is 1 unit. On a stool beside the quilt stand three lace reels with the lengths of your maths book: red lace 40 units, green lace 50 units and blue lace 25 units, each lace marked in units. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: tap a reel to pick its lace; drag the end of the lace along the border of the quilt, and it snaps to the patch edges, one unit for each patch side, and turns at the corners; a Cut button that cuts the lace at the place reached; an Undo button that picks the lace up one unit at a time; a Two laces switch that gives a second reel slot, so that a second colour can be laid after the first one is cut; Check, Hint, Retry (picks up the lace of this step), Reset (returns the quilt and the three reels), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: a counter units laid (for example 25), the units left to cover (for example 25 left), the length of the reel chosen, and a card number out of 7. On the small practice quilt the student taps each outer edge and a counter adds one for each tap.
student_does: Look at Grandmother's quilt and the three lace reels from the story. She wants to put lace all the way round the edge of the quilt. Tap the reel you think will go all the way round, then press Next.

Lay each lace along the border from the top left corner and watch where it ends, count the units on each side, count the border of a small practice quilt edge by edge, and see why counting the patches along the border is not the same as counting the lace units.

Answer Grandmother's own questions from the story: Tick the lace option that would cover the entire border of the quilt. She decides to use two different coloured laces. How much lace of each kind will be needed to cover the entire border? Cut two laces that go all the way round.
challenges: Card 1: pick the blue lace and drag it along the border from the top left corner. Where does it run out? Answer: after 25 units, at the bottom right corner, because the top side is 15 units and the right side is 10 units and 15 + 10 = 25. The bottom side and the left side are not covered, so the blue lace is too short.

Card 2: pick the red lace and lay it the same way. Where does it run out? Answer: after 40 units, at the bottom left corner, because 15 + 10 + 15 = 40. The left side, 10 units, is still not covered, so the red lace is too short.
Card 3: pick the green lace and lay it all the way round. What do the four sides add up to? Answer: 15 + 10 + 15 + 10 = 50 units. The green lace is 50 units, so it fits all the way round exactly.
Card 4 (practice values): a small quilt of 6 patches by 4 patches. Tap every outer edge once and read the counter. Answer: 6 + 4 + 6 + 4 = 20, so the border has 20 units.

Card 5: count the patches along the border of the big quilt, then count the units of lace. Why are the two numbers different? Answer: the patches on the border are 46 and the lace units are 50, because each of the 4 corner patches has 2 sides on the border but is counted once as a patch: 46 + 4 = 50. Count the units of lace, not the patches.

Challenge: 'Tick the lace option that would cover the entire border of the quilt. (i) Red lace 40 units (ii) Green lace 50 units (iii) Blue lace 25 units.' Lay each lace and tick the one that covers the entire border. Answer: (ii) the green lace, 50 units, because the border is 15 + 10 + 15 + 10 = 50 units; the red lace and the blue lace are too short.

Challenge: 'She decides to use two different coloured laces. How much lace of each kind will be needed to cover the entire border?' Turn on Two laces, lay the first lace, cut it, then lay a lace of a different colour to finish the border. Answer: any two lengths that make 50 units in all and fit the reels are right, for example 30 units of red lace for the two long sides and 20 units of blue lace for the two short sides, because 30 + 20 = 50, or 25 units of blue lace and 25 units of red lace. Your answer may differ. Next stop: the name for the length of the border.
feedback: The lace follows the finger along the patch edges and the counter units laid goes up one for each patch side. When a reel runs out the lace stops with a soft note, for example: The red lace has 40 units. The border is longer, 10 units still to cover.
When a lace goes all the way round exactly, the quilt shines softly and the tool names the sides: 15, 10, 15 and 10 units.

A tap on an outer edge of the practice quilt lights it orange and adds one to the counter. An edge that is inside the quilt gives a soft amber note: This edge is inside. Count the edges on the outside.

In the two-lace challenge the tool accepts any split that covers the whole border, and says for example: 30 units of red and 20 units of blue make 50 units, the whole border. If the lace is too long for a reel it says: The blue reel has only 25 units.
A wrong tick shows a soft amber note and never a red cross, and it asks the student to lay that lace along the border and look again.
tool_config.done_when: The student has laid the red, blue and green laces along the border and seen which one is long enough, has counted the border of the small quilt edge by edge, has seen why the patches on the border are fewer than the units of lace, and has ticked the right lace and cut two laces for the border.

hint_ladder.text: What does the lace have to go round? Look at the edge of the quilt, all the way round.
Count the lace units along one side of the quilt, one unit for each patch side. Then count the next side.
The long side is 15 units and the short side is 10 units. How many long sides and how many short sides does the border have? Add them all.
15 + 10 + 15 + 10 = 50. The border is 50 units, so the lace must be 50 units or more. The tool lays the first side so you can see it.

concepts.concept_name: Perimeter: The Border of a Shape

content.text: Recall that the length of the border of a shape is called its perimeter.
content.publication_text: Recall that the length of the border of a shape is called its perimeter.
lines: Recall that the length of the border of a shape is called its perimeter.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a mat is 8 patches long and 3 patches broad, and each patch side is 1 unit. How much lace goes all the way round its edge?
2. The edge of a shape is its border. The length of the border is called the perimeter.
3. To find it, walk once round the border and add the length of every side. For the mat: 8 + 3 + 8 + 3 = 22, so 22 units of lace.
4. When all the sides of a shape are equal, count the sides and multiply by one side. A shape with 3 equal sides of 6 cm has a perimeter of 3 × 6 = 18 cm.
5. Rule: the perimeter is the length of the whole border, found by adding all the sides.

The edge of a shape is its border. The length of the border is called the perimeter.
To find it, walk once round the border and add the length of every side. For the mat: 8 + 3 + 8 + 3 = 22, so 22 units of lace.
When all the sides of a shape are equal, count the sides and multiply by one side. A shape with 3 equal sides of 6 cm has a perimeter of 3 × 6 = 18 cm.

content.text:
Worked example: A mat has 5 equal sides, and each side is 7 cm long. Grandmother wants to sew a lace all the way round its border. How long is the lace?
1. The border is the line all the way round the mat, so we add the length of all 5 sides.
2. 7 + 7 + 7 + 7 + 7 = 35.
3. All the sides are equal, so we can also multiply: 5 sides of 7 cm make 5 × 7 = 35.
4. Check: adding and multiplying both give 35, so the lace must be 35 cm long.
Answer: The perimeter is 35 cm, so the lace is 35 cm long

content.question: Preetha and Adrit's grandmother made a quilt cover using old clothes. Now she wants to decorate it with lace. Tick the lace option that would cover the entire border of the quilt. (i) Red lace 40 units (ii) Green lace 50 units (iii) Blue lace 25 units
steps: The border is the line all the way round the quilt. Count one unit of lace for each patch side along it.
One long side has 15 patches, so it needs 15 units. One short side has 10 patches, so it needs 10 units.
The quilt has 2 long sides and 2 short sides: 15 + 10 + 15 + 10 = 50.
The border is 50 units long.
Red lace is 40 units and 40 is less than 50, so it is too short. Blue lace is 25 units and 25 is less than 50, so it is too short.
Green lace is 50 units, exactly the length of the border.
content.answer: (ii) Green lace, 50 units, because the border is 15 + 10 + 15 + 10 = 50 units.

content.question: She decides to use two different coloured laces. How much lace of each kind will be needed to cover the entire border?
steps: The whole border is 50 units: 15 + 10 + 15 + 10 = 50.
Use one colour for the two long sides and the other colour for the two short sides.
The two long sides need 15 + 15 = 30 units. Use 30 units of the red lace, because the red reel has 40 units.
The two short sides need 10 + 10 = 20 units. Use 20 units of the blue lace, because the blue reel has 25 units.
Check: 30 + 20 = 50, the whole border.
Another split works too: 25 units of blue lace and 25 units of red lace, because 25 + 25 = 50. Your answer may differ.
content.answer: Sample answer: 30 units of red lace and 20 units of blue lace, because 30 + 20 = 50. Your answer may differ.

content.question: Find the perimeter of the following shapes. All sides of the following shapes are equal. (a) the shape on the left, with a side of 4 cm; (b) the shape on the right, with a side of 5 cm
steps: (a) The shape on the left has 5 sides, and every side is 4 cm.
Add the sides: 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 20.
All the sides are equal, so multiply: 5 × 4 = 20. The perimeter is 20 cm.
(b) The shape on the right has 4 sides, and every side is 5 cm.
Add the sides: 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 20.
All the sides are equal, so multiply: 4 × 5 = 20. The perimeter is 20 cm.
Check: for each shape, adding and multiplying give the same number.

content.text:
1. Predict first: Preetha covers a table top with circles and Adrit covers one with squares. Whose table top will have gaps?
2. A tile is a shape used to cover a surface. Tiles must fit together with no gaps and no overlaps.
3. Squares fit edge to edge with no gaps. Rectangles fit the same way. Triangles fit too: one table top in your maths book is covered by triangles with no gaps.
4. Circles do not tile. Between round tiles there are always gaps, and to close the gaps the circles would have to overlap.
5. Rule: squares, rectangles and triangles tile a surface; circles leave gaps.

content.text:
Worked example: Grandmother wants to cover a tray top with identical tiles. She tries 12 square tiles in 3 rows of 4, and 6 round tiles in 2 rows of 3. Which tiles cover the tray with no gaps and no overlaps?
1. Squares first: 3 rows of 4 squares, 3 × 4 = 12 squares.
2. The squares meet edge to edge, so there are no gaps and no overlaps: squares tile.
3. Now the round tiles: 2 rows of 3 circles, 2 × 3 = 6 circles.
4. There are gaps between the circles and at the corners of the tray. Pushing the circles together to close the gaps would make them overlap.
5. Check: only the squares cover the tray with no gaps and no overlaps.
Answer: The square tiles cover the tray exactly; the round tiles leave gaps

content.text:
1. Predict first: a table top is covered by 20 triangles. What do we call the amount of table top that the triangles cover?
2. The region that the tiles cover is called the area. To find the area, count the tiles.
3. Say the tile in the unit: 20 triangles make an area of 20 triangle units, and 8 squares make an area of 8 square units.
4. The same region can be covered with different tiles. Preetha covers her desk with squares, then with triangles: the triangles are more in number, because each square is cut into 2 triangles.
5. Rule: the area is the number of tiles that cover the region, counted in the unit of the tile. A different tile gives a different count.

content.text:
Worked example: A tray top is covered by 24 square tiles in 4 rows of 6. Every square is then cut from corner to corner into 2 triangles, and the same tray top is covered with the triangles. What is the area of the tray top in square units and in triangle units?
1. Count the squares: 4 rows of 6, 4 × 6 = 24 squares. The area is 24 square units.
2. Each square makes 2 triangles, so the triangles are 24 × 2 = 48.
3. The same tray top is covered by 48 triangles. The area is 48 triangle units.
4. The region did not change, only the tile did, so a different tile gives a different count.
5. Check: 48 ÷ 2 = 24, so 2 triangles make 1 square.
Answer: The area is 24 square units, which is 48 triangle units

tool_config.screen: The table corner of Grandmother's patchwork room, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. Four table tops stand in a row, Table 1, Table 2, Table 3 and Table 4, as in your maths book, and the table being covered is the largest thing on screen, in the middle. Table 1 takes triangles (each square of a 5 by 2 top is cut from corner to corner into 2 triangles), Table 2 takes circles (a 4 by 2 top), Table 3 takes squares (a 4 by 2 top) and Table 4 takes rectangles (a 3 by 4 top). Preetha's desk is a 9 by 6 grid of equal squares with three tiles for it: a blue square, a green triangle that is half a square and a red triangle whose two shorter sides are each 3 squares long. Controls: tap a tile on the shelf and then tap places on the table to put the tile down; a Fill the rest button that repeats the tile over the empty places; an Undo button; a Gaps glow that turns the empty spaces between tiles soft orange; Check, Hint, Retry (clears the table in front), Reset (returns all the tables and the desk), Back and Next in the same places on every card. student_does: Look at Grandmother's rug of square patches from the story, with its rows and columns of patches. Tap the shapes you think can cover a table top with no gaps and no overlaps, then press Next.

challenges: Card 1: pick the triangle and cover Table 1. How many triangles cover it? Answer: 20 triangles, because the table has 5 by 2 squares, 10 squares, and each square is 2 triangles, 10 × 2 = 20. So the area of Table 1 is 20 triangle units.

Card 3: pick the rectangle and cover Table 4. How many rectangles cover it? Answer: 12 rectangles, because 3 × 4 = 12. The area of Table 4 is 12 rectangle units.

Card 5 (practice values): a tray of 6 squares by 4 squares. Cover it with square tiles, then with triangle tiles, each square cut from corner to corner. Answer: 24 squares, because 6 × 4 = 24, and 48 triangles, because 24 × 2 = 48. The tray did not change, only the tile did.

Answer: triangle, square and rectangle shapes cover the table, and the circle shape leaves gaps. 20 triangles, 8 squares and 12 rectangles, so the areas are 20 triangle units, 8 square units and 12 rectangle units.

Cover the desk with each tile in turn. steps: Look at the rug. The patches are in rows, and every row has the same number of patches.
Count the rows: there are 6 rows.
Count the patches in one row: there are 15 patches.
Check by columns: there are 15 columns of 6 patches, and 15 × 6 = 90.
content.answer: 90 patches
content.text:
1. Look at the rug. The patches are in rows, and every row has the same number of patches.
2. Count the rows: there are $6$ rows.
3. Count the patches in one row: there are $15$ patches.
4. Add the rows: $15 + 15 + 15 + 15 + 15 + 15 = 90$. Or multiply: $6 \times 15 = 90$.
5. Check by columns: there are $15$ columns of $6$ patches, and $15 \times 6 = 90$.
Answer: $90$ patches

content.question: Do circles tile? Can we use them to cover a region?
steps: Look at Table 2. It is covered by 8 circles, 4 in a row and 2 rows.
There are gaps between the circles and at the edges of the table.
To close the gaps the circles would have to overlap each other.
A shape tiles only when there are no gaps and no overlaps, so circles do not tile.
Check: squares, rectangles and triangles left no gaps, but the circles did.
content.answer: No. Circles leave gaps, so they do not tile and cannot cover a region without gaps or overlaps.

content.book_number: Tiles and Tables: cover your own table
content.question: Now, try to cover the top of your table without gaps and overlaps with the following objects of same size. (a) Notebooks (b) Lunch boxes (c) Pencil boxes (d) Maths books. Which of the above objects covered the region completely?
steps: Notebooks, lunch boxes, pencil boxes and maths books are all rectangles. Rectangles tile: they fit side by side with no gaps and no overlaps.
So each of the four objects can cover a table top without gaps and overlaps if you lay it in neat rows.
Whether an object covers the table completely depends on the table: its length and breadth must hold a whole number of the objects.
Sample answer with practice values: a notebook 20 cm long and 15 cm broad, and a table top 60 cm long and 30 cm broad.
Along the length: 60 ÷ 20 = 3 notebooks. Along the breadth: 30 ÷ 15 = 2 notebooks.
3 × 2 = 6 notebooks cover this table top completely.
Your answer may differ, because your table and your objects may be different sizes.

content.question: Preetha is playing with tiles. She covers her desk with different shapes as shown below. Look at the different tiles on her desk and answer how many of the following shapes will cover the desk. (a) Green triangles ___; (b) Red triangles ___; (c) Blue squares ___
steps: Count the squares of the desk: 9 squares in a row and 6 rows, 9 × 6 = 54 squares.
(a) A green triangle is half a square, so 2 green triangles cover 1 square.
54 × 2 = 108 green triangles cover the desk.
(b): 2 red triangles put together make a square 3 squares long and 3 squares broad, which is 9 squares.
The desk holds 9 ÷ 3 = 3 of these big squares in a row and 6 ÷ 3 = 2 rows, so 3 × 2 = 6 big squares.
Each big square is 2 red triangles: 6 × 2 = 12 red triangles cover the desk.
(c) A blue square is 1 square, so 54 blue squares cover the desk.
Check: 1 red triangle covers 9 green triangles, and 12 × 9 = 108, the same as the green count.
content.answer: (a): 108 green triangles; (b): 12 red triangles; (c): 54 blue squares

content.text: Which of the above rectangles has the largest area? Trace these shapes on to a paper and cut them to find out the one that has the largest area.

lines: Which of the above rectangles has the largest area? Trace these shapes on to a paper and cut them to find out the one that has the largest area.

content.text:
1. Predict first: rectangle A is wide and short and rectangle C is narrow and tall. Which one has the larger area, and how could you find out?
2. If one shape fits inside the other, the shape that fits inside has the smaller area. Trace it, cut it out and lay it on the other.
3. Sometimes neither shape fits inside the other. A is wider but C is taller, so laying one on the other does not settle it.
4. Then cover both shapes with the same small square and count the squares. The shape with more squares has the larger area.
5. Rule: compare areas by laying one on the other when one fits inside, and by counting equal squares when it does not.

content.text:
Worked example: Mat P is 7 squares long and 2 squares broad. Mat Q is 4 squares long and 4 squares broad. Which mat has the larger area?
1. Lay mat Q on mat P. Q is shorter than P in length, but Q is broader. Neither mat fits inside the other, so laying them does not settle it.
2. Cover both with the same square tiles and count. Mat P has 2 rows of 7 squares: 2 × 7 = 14 squares.
3. Mat Q has 4 rows of 4 squares: 4 × 4 = 16 squares.
4. 16 is more than 14, so mat Q has the larger area.
5. Check: Q is not the longer mat, yet it has the larger area, so length alone cannot decide.
Answer: Mat Q has the larger area: 16 squares is more than 14 squares

concepts.concept_name: The Unit Square and Counting Squares

content.text: Using square grids is the most convenient way to find the area of regions. We say that the area of a square with sides 1 unit is 1 unit square.
content.publication_text: Using square grids is the most convenient way to find the area of regions. We say that the area of a square with sides 1 unit is 1 unit square.
lines: Using square grids is the most convenient way to find the area of regions. We say that the area of a square with sides 1 unit is 1 unit square.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a shape on a grid covers 6 whole squares and 4 half squares. How many squares is that in all?
2. The most convenient way to find an area is to put the shape on a square grid. A square with sides 1 unit has an area of 1 unit square.
3. When the sides are 1 cm, the area of the square is 1 square cm.
4. The area of a shape is the number of unit squares it covers. Count the whole squares first.
5. Two half squares together make 1 whole square, so put the half squares in pairs.
6. We choose a square as the unit because all its sides are equal, just as we measure a length with a unit of length.
7. Rule: the area is the number of unit squares that cover the shape, and two half squares make one.

content.text:
Worked example: A triangle is drawn on a grid of 1 cm squares. It covers 6 whole squares and 4 half squares. What is its area?
1. The area of a square with sides 1 cm is 1 square cm, so each whole square counts 1 square cm.
2. Count the whole squares: 6 whole squares are 6 square cm.
3. Count the half squares: there are 4, and 2 half squares make 1 whole square, so 4 ÷ 2 = 2 whole squares.
4. Add: 6 + 2 = 8.
5. Check: the 4 half squares match up in 2 pairs, so none is left over.
Answer: The area is 8 square cm

media.description: Concept video: Show how to compare two areas: lay one on the other when it fits inside, and count equal squares when neither fits inside the other. It works this example: Mat P is 7 squares long and 2 squares broad. Mat Q is 4 squares long and 4 squares broad. Which mat has the larger area?
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: rectangle A is wide and short and rectangle C is narrow and tall. Which one has the larger area, and how could you find out? If one shape fits inside the other, the shape that fits inside has the smaller area. Trace it, cut it out and lay it on the other. Sometimes neither shape fits inside the other. A is wider but C is taller, so laying one on the other does not settle it. Then cover both shapes with the same small square and count the squares. The shape with more squares has the larger area. Rule: compare areas by laying one on the other when one fits inside, and by counting equal squares when it does not. 1. Lay mat Q on mat P. Q is shorter than P in length, but Q is broader. Neither mat fits inside the other, so laying them does not settle it. 2. Cover both with the same square tiles and count. Mat P has 2 rows of 7 squares: 2 × 7 = 14 squares. 3. Mat Q has 4 rows of 4 squares: 4 × 4 = 16 squares. 4. 16 is more than 14, so mat Q has the larger area. 5. Check: Q is not the longer mat, yet it has the larger area, so length alone cannot decide. Answer: Mat Q has the larger area: 16 squares is more than 14 squares

media.teaching_notes: Predict first: a shape on a grid covers 6 whole squares and 4 half squares. How many squares is that in all? The most convenient way to find an area is to put the shape on a square grid. A square with sides 1 unit has an area of 1 unit square. When the sides are 1 cm, the area of the square is 1 square cm. The area of a shape is the number of unit squares it covers. Count the whole squares first. Two half squares together make 1 whole square, so put the half squares in pairs. We choose a square as the unit because all its sides are equal, just as we measure a length with a unit of length. Rule: the area is the number of unit squares that cover the shape, and two half squares make one. 1. The area of a square with sides 1 cm is 1 square cm, so each whole square counts 1 square cm. 2. Count the whole squares: 6 whole squares are 6 square cm. 3. Count the half squares: there are 4, and 2 half squares make 1 whole square, so 4 ÷ 2 = 2 whole squares. 4. Add: 6 + 2 = 8. 5. Check: the 4 half squares match up in 2 pairs, so none is left over. Answer: The area is 8 square cm

content.question: Which of the above rectangles has the largest area? Trace these shapes on to a paper and cut them to find out the one that has the largest area.
steps: Trace the three rectangles on paper and cut them out.
Lay B on A: B fits inside A, so the area of A is larger than the area of B.
Lay B on C: B fits inside C, so the area of C is larger than the area of B. So B is the smallest.
Lay A on C: neither fits inside the other, because A is wider and C is taller. Cutting alone does not tell us.
Put the rectangles on a square grid and count the unit squares: A has 3 × 4 = 12, C has 2 × 5 = 10 and B has 2 × 4 = 8.
12 is the most, so A has the largest area.
Check: 12 is more than 10, and 10 is more than 8.
content.answer: A has the largest area: 12 unit squares, against 10 for C and 8 for B.

content.question: Let us put these rectangles on a square grid. Now, can you identify the rectangle that has the largest area?
steps: On the grid every square is 1 unit square, so the area is the number of squares covered.
A covers 3 columns and 4 rows: 3 × 4 = 12 squares.
B covers 2 columns and 4 rows: 2 × 4 = 8 squares.
C covers 2 columns and 5 rows: 2 × 5 = 10 squares.
12 is more than 10, and 10 is more than 8, so A has the largest area, then C, then B.
Check: count A again by columns: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.
content.answer: Yes. A covers 12 unit squares, B covers 8 and C covers 10, so A has the largest area.

content.question: Compare the areas of the two gardens given below on the square grid. Share your observations. Area of Garden A: ___ square cm. Area of Garden B: ___ square cm.
steps: Garden A is 2 columns wide and 5 rows tall, so each row has 2 squares.
5 rows of 2 squares: 5 × 2 = 10. The area of garden A is 10 square cm.
Garden B is 4 columns wide and 3 rows tall, so each row has 4 squares.
3 rows of 4 squares: 3 × 4 = 12. The area of garden B is 12 square cm.
12 is more than 10, so garden B has the larger area, by 12 − 10 = 2 square cm.
The pale strip is part of neither garden, so it is not counted.
Check: count garden A square by square: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10.
content.answer: Garden A: 10 square cm. Garden B: 12 square cm. Garden B has the larger area.

content.question: Trace your palm on the square grid given below and find the approximate area of your palm. Compare the area of your palm with your friend's palm. Who has a bigger palm?
steps: Put your hand flat on the grid and trace round it with a pencil. Each square of the grid is 1 square cm.
Count the whole squares inside the outline.
Then look at the squares that are only partly inside. Put them together in your mind: two part squares make about 1 whole square.
Add the whole squares and the squares made from the parts. This is the approximate area of your palm.
Do the same for your friend's palm and compare the two numbers: the bigger number is the bigger palm.
Sample answer with practice values: my palm has 54 whole squares and 12 part squares, which make about 6 whole squares, so the area is about 54 + 6 = 60 square cm.
My friend's palm is about 48 square cm. 60 is more than 48, so my palm is bigger. Your answer may differ.

content.question: Collect leaves of different kinds. Put them on a square grid and find their area. (a) Name the leaf with the largest area. (b) Name the leaf with the smallest area.
steps: Collect a few different leaves and lay each one flat on the square grid. Trace its outline.
For each leaf count the whole squares inside, then put the part squares together to make about whole squares, and add. This gives the area of the leaf.
Compare the numbers: the leaf with the biggest number has the largest area, and the leaf with the smallest number has the smallest area.
Sample answer with practice values: leaf P is about 30 square cm, leaf Q about 18 square cm and leaf R about 24 square cm.
(a) The largest area is 30 square cm, leaf P.
(b) The smallest area is 18 square cm, leaf Q.
Check: 18 is less than 24 and 24 is less than 30. Your answer may differ.
content.answer: Sample answer with practice values: (a): leaf P, 30 square cm; (b): leaf Q, 18 square cm. Your answer may differ.

media.teaching_notes: 1. Put your hand flat on the grid and trace round it with a pencil. Each square of the grid is 1 square cm. 2. Count the whole squares inside the outline. 3. Then look at the squares that are only partly inside. Put them together in your mind: two part squares make about 1 whole square. 4. Add the whole squares and the squares made from the parts. This is the approximate area of your palm. 5. Do the same for your friend's palm and compare the two numbers: the bigger number is the bigger palm. 6. Sample answer with practice values: my palm has 54 whole squares and 12 part squares, which make about 6 whole squares, so the area is about 54 + 6 = 60 square cm. 7. My friend's palm is about 48 square cm. 60 is more than 48, so my palm is bigger. Your answer may differ. Answer: Sample answer: my palm is about 60 square cm and my friend's is about 48 square cm, so my palm is bigger. Your answer may differ.

modules.module_summary: Seeing that area and perimeter are different measures, finding the area and the perimeter of rectangles and squares with the book's rules, and using the rules for a missing side, a side given in parts and real objects.

content.text:
1. Predict first: three rectangles are each made of 16 unit squares. Will they all have the same perimeter?
2. Area counts the squares inside a shape. Perimeter counts the edges all the way round it. They are two different measures.
3. A square 4 by 4, a rectangle 8 by 2 and a thin strip 16 by 1 are all made of 16 squares. Their borders are not the same length.
4. The long thin shape has the longest border, because its squares are spread out along its sides.
5. Rule: shapes with the same area can have different perimeters.

content.text:
Worked example: Three rectangles are each made of 16 unit squares: 4 by 4, 8 by 2 and 16 by 1. Find the area and the perimeter of each.
1. Areas: 4 × 4 = 16, 8 × 2 = 16 and 16 × 1 = 16. All three have the same area, 16 square units.
2. Perimeter of the 4 by 4 rectangle: 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16 units.
3. Perimeter of the 8 by 2 rectangle: 8 + 2 + 8 + 2 = 20 units.
4. Perimeter of the 16 by 1 rectangle: 16 + 1 + 16 + 1 = 34 units.
5. Check: 16, 20 and 34 are three different numbers.
Answer: All three have an area of 16 square units, but the perimeters are 16, 20 and 34 units

content.text:
1. Predict first: Trisha makes a bigger rectangle, so its area grows. Must its perimeter grow too?
2. Shapes can also have the same perimeter and different areas. The area depends on how many squares fit inside the border, not on how long the border is.
3. Compare a 1 by 8 rectangle with a 3 by 3 square. The 1 by 8 rectangle has area 1 × 8 = 8 and perimeter 1 + 8 + 1 + 8 = 18. The 3 by 3 square has area 3 × 3 = 9 and perimeter 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12.
4. The area grew from 8 to 9, but the perimeter became smaller, from 18 to 12.
5. Rule: area and perimeter are different measures. One can stay the same while the other changes, so a bigger area does not always mean a bigger perimeter.

content.text:
Worked example: Three rectangles each have a perimeter of 20 units: 5 by 5, 7 by 3 and 9 by 1. Find the area of each.
1. Check the perimeters first: 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 20, 7 + 3 + 7 + 3 = 20 and 9 + 1 + 9 + 1 = 20.
2. Area of the 5 by 5 rectangle: 5 × 5 = 25 square units.
3. Area of the 7 by 3 rectangle: 7 × 3 = 21 square units.
4. Area of the 9 by 1 rectangle: 9 × 1 = 9 square units.
5. Check: 25, 21 and 9 are different, though the perimeter is 20 for all three.
Answer: The perimeter is 20 units for all three, but the areas are 25, 21 and 9 square units

media.title: Shape Builder

tool_config.title: Shape Builder
tool_config.idea: Build shapes on a square grid and read the area and the perimeter side by side, to see that shapes with the same area can have different perimeters, that shapes with the same perimeter can have different areas, and that a bigger area does not always give a bigger perimeter.
tool_config.screen: Grandmother's patchwork board, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. A big grid of 15 columns by 12 rows of equal unit squares lies on the table and is the largest thing on screen, with a box of loose unit patches beside it. Two read-outs sit above the grid: Area, the number of squares inside the shape, and Perimeter, the number of edges all the way round it, with the outline of the shape drawn thick. A shelf below the grid keeps up to 3 saved shapes, each with its Area and Perimeter written on it. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: tap a square to place a patch and tap it again to take it away; drag across squares to place several at once; a Save shape button that puts the shape on the shelf; a Show outline switch that lights the outer edges one by one as they are counted; a Clear button; Check, Hint, Undo, Retry (clears the grid of this step), Reset (clears the grid and the shelf), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: Area (squares), Perimeter (edges), the saved shapes on the shelf, and a card number out of 7.
student_does: Look at a rug of 2 by 3 patches with its Area 6 and its Perimeter 10 shown. Count the patches inside, then count the edges round the outside, and say which number is which.

Build three rectangles of the same area and read their perimeters, build three rectangles of the same perimeter and read their areas, and find two shapes where the area goes up and the perimeter goes down.

Answer the book's own questions: Trisha's two rectangles and her claim, which shapes have the same area and what their perimeters are, which shapes have the same perimeter and what their areas are, and drawing different shapes with the same area as the given shape.
challenges: Card 1 (practice values): build a 4 by 4 rectangle, an 8 by 2 rectangle and a 16 by 1 rectangle, and save each one. What do you notice? Answer: all three have an area of 16 square units, because 4 × 4 = 16, 8 × 2 = 16 and 16 × 1 = 16, but the perimeters are different: 16, 20 and 34 units.

Card 2 (practice values): build a 5 by 5, a 7 by 3 and a 9 by 1 rectangle, and save each one. What do you notice? Answer: all three have a perimeter of 20 units, because 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 20, 7 + 3 + 7 + 3 = 20 and 9 + 1 + 9 + 1 = 20, but the areas are different: 25, 21 and 9 square units.

Card 3 (practice values): build a 1 by 8 rectangle and then a 3 by 3 square. Which number goes up and which goes down? Answer: the area goes up, from 1 × 8 = 8 to 3 × 3 = 9, and the perimeter goes down, from 18 to 12. A bigger area does not always give a bigger perimeter.

Challenge: 'Trisha makes these two rectangles. She says, "I increased the area of my rectangle, and the perimeter increased." Do you think this is always true?' Build her two rectangles, 2 squares by 3 and 3 squares by 4, and then try 5 by 2 and 4 by 3. Answer: for her rectangles the area grows from 6 to 12 and the perimeter from 10 to 14, but 5 by 2 and 4 by 3 have areas 10 and 12 and the same perimeter, 14. No, it is not always true.

Challenge: 'Tick the shapes with the same area. Find the perimeters of these shapes. What do you notice?' The six shapes (a) to (f) are on the grid. Answer: (a), (b), (c), (d) and (f) have an area of 12 square cm, and their perimeters are 16, 18, 14, 14 and 26 cm. Shape (e) has an area of 8. The same area can have different perimeters.

Challenge: 'Tick the shapes with the same perimeter. Find the areas of these shapes. What do you notice?' The five shapes (a) to (e) are on the grid. Answer: (a) and (b) have a perimeter of 12 cm and (c), (d) and (e) have a perimeter of 16 cm. Every shape has an area of 7 square cm.

Challenge: 'Draw different shapes having the same area as the given shape. Write the perimeter of each shape. What do you notice?' The given shape is 9 squares by 2 and has an area of 18. Answer: any shape of exactly 18 squares is right, for example 6 by 3 with a perimeter of 18 cm, or 18 by 1 with a perimeter of 38 cm; the given shape has a perimeter of 22 cm. The perimeters are not all the same. Your answer may differ.

hint_ladder.text: What does each number count? Area counts the squares inside, and perimeter counts the edges round the outside.
Count the squares of the shape first, then walk round the outside and count the edges.
Compare the two numbers for each shape. Which one stayed the same and which one changed?
For a 4 by 4 shape: 4 × 4 = 16 squares, and 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16 edges. The tool builds it and counts the edges so you can see them.

tool_questions: Card 1 (practice values): build a 4 by 4 rectangle, an 8 by 2 rectangle and a 16 by 1 rectangle, and save each one. What do you notice? Answer: all three have an area of 16 square units, because 4 × 4 = 16, 8 × 2 = 16 and 16 × 1 = 16, but the perimeters are different: 16, 20 and 34 units.

Card 2 (practice values): build a 5 by 5, a 7 by 3 and a 9 by 1 rectangle, and save each one. What do you notice? Answer: all three have a perimeter of 20 units, because 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 20, 7 + 3 + 7 + 3 = 20 and 9 + 1 + 9 + 1 = 20, but the areas are different: 25, 21 and 9 square units.

Card 3 (practice values): build a 1 by 8 rectangle and then a 3 by 3 square. Which number goes up and which goes down? Answer: the area goes up, from 1 × 8 = 8 to 3 × 3 = 9, and the perimeter goes down, from 18 to 12. A bigger area does not always give a bigger perimeter.

Challenge: 'Trisha makes these two rectangles. She says, "I increased the area of my rectangle, and the perimeter increased." Do you think this is always true?' Build her two rectangles, 2 squares by 3 and 3 squares by 4, and then try 5 by 2 and 4 by 3. content.question: Is the area of shape (a) less than the area of shape (b) given below? Discuss.
steps: Shape (a) is a square 3 squares wide and 3 squares tall. Its area is 3 × 3 = 9 square units.
Shape (b) is a triangle. Count its whole squares row by row: the top row has 4 whole squares, the next row has 2 and the last row has 0: 4 + 2 + 0 = 6 whole squares.
Count its half squares: each row has 2, so there are 6 half squares. 2 half squares make 1 whole square, so 6 ÷ 2 = 3 whole squares.
The area of shape (b) is 6 + 3 = 9 square units.
Shape (a) has 9 and shape (b) has 9, so the two areas are equal.
Check: 9 is not less than 9, so the area of (a) is not less than the area of (b).
content.answer: No. Shape (a) has 9 unit squares. Shape (b) has 6 whole squares and 6 half squares, which is also 9. The areas are equal.

content.book_number: Trisha's Rectangles: is it always true
content.question: Trisha makes these two rectangles. She says, "I increased the area of my rectangle, and the perimeter increased." Do you think this is always true?
steps: First rectangle: 2 squares wide and 3 squares tall. Area: 2 × 3 = 6 square units. Perimeter: 2 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 10 units.
Second rectangle: 3 squares wide and 4 squares tall. Area: 3 × 4 = 12 square units. Perimeter: 3 + 4 + 3 + 4 = 14 units.
Here the area grew from 6 to 12 and the perimeter grew from 10 to 14. Trisha is right for these two rectangles.
But is it always true? Look at the two mats: the area grew from 10 to 12, and the perimeter stayed 14.

Try one more pair. A 1 by 8 rectangle has area 1 × 8 = 8 and perimeter 1 + 8 + 1 + 8 = 18. A 3 by 3 square has area 3 × 3 = 9 and perimeter 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12. The area grew and the perimeter became smaller.
So a bigger area does not always give a bigger perimeter.
Check: 18 is more than 12, so the perimeter went down while the area went up.
content.answer: No, it is not always true. Here both grew (area 6 to 12, perimeter 10 to 14), but the mats have areas 10 and 12 and the same perimeter 14.

content.question: Tick the shapes with the same area. Find the perimeters of these shapes. What do you notice? Discuss.
steps: Count the squares of each shape. (a) is 6 squares wide and 2 tall: 6 × 2 = 12 squares.
(b) is a block 2 wide and 5 tall, 2 × 5 = 10 squares, with a row of 2 more on top: 10 + 2 = 12 squares.
(c) is 3 wide and 4 tall: 3 × 4 = 12 squares. (d) is 4 wide and 3 tall: 4 × 3 = 12 squares.
(e) is a row of 8 squares, so its area is 8. (f) is a row of 12 squares, so its area is 12.
The shapes with the same area, 12 square cm, are (a), (b), (c), (d) and (f). Tick these five.
(b): the 2 by 5 block has 2 + 5 + 2 + 5 = 14 cm round it, and the row of 2 on top, shifted one square to the left, adds 4 more: 14 + 4 = 18 cm.
Notice: the five shapes all cover 12 square cm, but their perimeters 16, 18, 14, 14 and 26 cm are different. The same area can have different perimeters.
content.answer: Same area, 12 square cm: (a), (b), (c), (d), (f). Perimeters: 16, 18, 14, 14, 26 cm. Same area, different perimeters.
content.text:
1. Count the squares of each shape. $(a)$ is $6$ squares wide and $2$ tall: $6 \times 2 = 12$ squares.
2. $(b)$ is a block $2$ wide and $5$ tall, $2 \times 5 = 10$ squares, with a row of $2$ more on top: $10 + 2 = 12$ squares.
3. $(c)$ is $3$ wide and $4$ tall: $3 \times 4 = 12$ squares. $(d)$ is $4$ wide and $3$ tall: $4 \times 3 = 12$ squares.
4. $(e)$ is a row of $8$ squares, so its area is $8$. $(f)$ is a row of $12$ squares, so its area is $12$.
[Image: Let Us Explore: Ans1: solution]
5. The shapes with the same area, $12\text{ square cm}$, are $(a)$, $(b)$, $(c)$, $(d)$ and $(f)$. Tick these five.
6. Now find the perimeters. $(a)$: $6 + 2 + 6 + 2 = 16\text{ cm}$. $(c)$: $3 + 4 + 3 + 4 = 14\text{ cm}$. $(d)$: $4 + 3 + 4 + 3 = 14\text{ cm}$. $(f)$: $12 + 1 + 12 + 1 = 26\text{ cm}$.
7. $(b)$: the $2$ by $5$ block has $2 + 5 + 2 + 5 = 14\text{ cm}$ round it, and the row of $2$ on top, shifted one square to the left, adds $4$ more: $14 + 4 = 18\text{ cm}$.
8. For $(e)$: $8 + 1 + 8 + 1 = 18\text{ cm}$.
9. Notice: the five shapes all cover $12\text{ square cm}$, but their perimeters $16$, $18$, $14$, $14$ and $26\text{ cm}$ are different. The same area can have different perimeters.
Answer: Same area, $12\text{ square cm}$: $(a)$, $(b)$, $(c)$, $(d)$, $(f)$. Perimeters: $16$, $18$, $14$, $14$, $26\text{ cm}$. Same area, different perimeters.
[Image: Let Us Explore: Ans1: solution (continued)]

content.question: Tick the shapes with the same perimeter. Find the areas of these shapes. What do you notice? Discuss.
steps: Count the squares of each shape. Every shape is made of 7 squares, so every area is 7 square cm.
Now find the perimeter of each shape by walking round its border and counting the outer edges.
(a): 3 across the top, 3 down the right side, 1 back, 1 up, 2 back, 2 up the left side: 3 + 3 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 12 cm.
(b): 3 across the top, 1 down, 1 back, 2 down, 2 back, 3 up the left side: 3 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 12 cm.
(c): a column of 4 squares has 4 + 1 + 4 + 1 = 10 edges round it. Each of the 3 squares joined to its side hides 1 edge and shows 3 new edges, so each adds 2: 10 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 16 cm.
(d): 1 across the top, 4 down, 2 across, 1 down, 3 back along the bottom, 5 up the left side: 1 + 4 + 2 + 1 + 3 + 5 = 16 cm.
(e): a row of 7 squares has 7 + 1 + 7 + 1 = 16 cm.
Shapes (a) and (b) have the same perimeter, 12 cm. Shapes (c), (d) and (e) have the same perimeter, 16 cm. Tick these.
Notice: all five shapes have the area 7 square cm, but the perimeter is 12 cm for two of them and 16 cm for three. The same area can have different perimeters.
content.answer: Perimeter 12 cm: (a), (b). Perimeter 16 cm: (c), (d), (e). Every shape has an area of 7 square cm.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a patchwork has 5 rows with 8 patches in each row. Do we have to count the patches one by one to find how many there are?
2. No. Count by rows: the number of rows times the number of patches in a row. That is 5 × 8 = 40 patches.
3. The number of patches in a row is the length of the rectangle, and the number of rows is its breadth. Each patch is a unit square, so the area is the same number.
4. Rule: area of a rectangle = length × breadth. If the sides are in cm the area is in square cm, and if the sides are in m the area is in square m.
5. Rows times columns is multiplication: this is why area and multiplication go together.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a rectangle is 12 cm long and 5 cm broad. How many different side lengths do you need to measure to find its perimeter?
2. Only two. The opposite sides of a rectangle are equal: the two long sides are the same, and the two short sides are the same.
3. Walk round the border and add: length + length + breadth + breadth.
4. That is 2 lengths and 2 breadths, so the perimeter is 2 × length + 2 × breadth.
5. Half of the perimeter is length + breadth. This helps when you know the perimeter and want to find possible sides.
6. Rule: perimeter of a rectangle = 2 × length + 2 × breadth.

tool_config.title: Rectangle Maker
tool_config.idea: Set the length and the breadth of a rectangle and see the patches fill in rows, so that the area is the rows times the patches in a row (length × breadth), and walk round the border to see that the perimeter is 2 × length + 2 × breadth, with the square as a rectangle whose sides are equal.
tool_config.screen: Grandmother's rug frame, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. A rectangular frame on the table is the largest thing on screen, and unit patches are laid in it in rows. The length and the breadth of the rectangle are set from 1 to 12, and the side labels in cm sit along the edges. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: a stepper for the length and a stepper for the breadth, each with plus and minus buttons; a Fill rows button that lays the patches one row at a time; a Walk the border button that sends a small marker round the rectangle adding the four sides; a Show the rule switch that writes Length × Breadth and 2 × Length + 2 × Breadth under the read-outs; answer boxes that take a number for a length, a breadth, an area or a perimeter in the challenge cards; Check, Hint, Undo, Retry (returns the rectangle of this step), Reset (returns the first rectangle), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the rows of patches (for example 5 rows of 8), Area in square cm, the sum of the four sides while the marker walks, Perimeter in cm, a Square badge that lights when the length and the breadth are equal, and a card number out of 7.
student_does: Look at 5 rows of 4 patches (practice values) with the count 20 shown. Say how many rows there are and how many patches are in a row, and how you could find the total without counting one by one.

Answer the book's own questions: draw two rectangles of the perimeters 26 cm and 18 cm, find the area and the perimeter of the five shapes on the grid, and find the area of the patchwork of 6 rows of 4 patches and the area and perimeter of a square with sides of 5 units.
challenges: Card 1 (practice values): make a rectangle with the length 8 and the breadth 5. What are its area and its perimeter? Answer: 5 rows of 8 patches, 5 × 8 = 40, so the area is 40 square cm. The perimeter is 8 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 26 cm.

Card 2 (practice values): change the breadth of that rectangle to 6. What happens to the area and the perimeter? Answer: the area becomes 8 × 6 = 48 square cm and the perimeter becomes 8 + 6 + 8 + 6 = 28 cm. Both numbers change.

Card 3 (practice values): make a square with a side of 9. What are its area and its perimeter? Answer: the Square badge lights, because the length and the breadth are equal. The area is 9 × 9 = 81 square cm and the perimeter is 4 × 9 = 36 cm.

Card 4 (practice values): make a rectangle with a perimeter of 20 cm and a length of 7 cm. What is its breadth? Answer: half of 20 is 10, and 7 + 3 = 10, so the breadth is 3 cm. Check: 2 × 7 = 14, 2 × 3 = 6 and 14 + 6 = 20.

Challenge: 'Draw two rectangles each having the following perimeters. (a) 26 cm (b) 18 cm.' Make two different rectangles for each perimeter. Answer: for (a) the length and the breadth must add to 13, for example 8 by 5 and 10 by 3; for (b) they must add to 9, for example 6 by 3 and 7 by 2. Your answer may differ.

Challenge: 'Find the area and perimeter of the following shapes.' The five shapes (a) to (e) are on the grid with a blank for the length and the breadth of each. Answer: (a) 6 by 6, area 36 square cm, perimeter 24 cm; (b) 4 by 7, area 28 square cm, perimeter 22 cm; (c) 12 by 4, area 48 square cm, perimeter 32 cm; (d) 3 by 3, area 9 square cm, perimeter 12 cm; (e) 6 by 5, area 30 square cm, perimeter 22 cm.

Challenge: the patchwork of 6 rows of 4 patches, and a square whose sides are 5 units long. Find the area of the patchwork, and the area and the perimeter of the square. Answer: 6 × 4 = 24 patches, so the area is 24 square cm; the square has an area of 5 × 5 = 25 square cm and a perimeter of 4 × 5 = 20 cm.

media.description: Concept video: Show that a square is a rectangle with equal sides, so its area is length times length and its perimeter is 4 times the length. It works this example: A square patch has a side of 7 cm. Find its area and its perimeter.
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: all the sides of a square patch are equal. How many lengths do you need to measure? Only one. A square is a rectangle whose length and breadth are equal. Area of a square = length × length: the side times itself. Perimeter of a square = length + length + length + length = 4 × length. Do not mix them up: the area is the side times itself, and the perimeter is 4 times the side. Rule: area of a square = length × length, and perimeter of a square = 4 × length. 1. All the sides of a square are equal, so the length and the breadth are both 7 cm. 2. Area = Length × Length = 7 × 7 = 49 square cm. 3. Perimeter = 4 × Length = 4 × 7 = 28 cm. 4. Check: adding the four sides, 7 + 7 + 7 + 7 = 28. Answer: The area is 49 square cm and the perimeter is 28 cm

content.question: Draw two rectangles each having the following perimeters. (a): 26 cm; (b): 18 cm
steps: The perimeter of a rectangle is 2 × length + 2 × breadth, so length + breadth is half of the perimeter.
(a) Half of 26 is 26 ÷ 2 = 13, so length + breadth = 13.
Choose a length and a breadth that add to 13: 8 + 5 = 13 and 10 + 3 = 13. Draw a rectangle 8 cm by 5 cm and another 10 cm by 3 cm.
(b) Half of 18 is 18 ÷ 2 = 9, so length + breadth = 9.
Choose 6 + 3 = 9 and 7 + 2 = 9. Draw a rectangle 6 cm by 3 cm and another 7 cm by 2 cm.
Check: 6 + 3 + 6 + 3 = 18 and 7 + 2 + 7 + 2 = 18. Your rectangles may be different.
content.answer: Sample answer: (a): 8 cm by 5 cm and 10 cm by 3 cm; (b): 6 cm by 3 cm and 7 cm by 2 cm. Your answer may differ.

4. Check: $8 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 26$ and $10 + 3 + 10 + 3 = 26$.

content.question: Find the area of your classroom floor in square meters. Take the help of your teacher to measure the length and breadth of the floor. What is the perimeter of the classroom floor?
steps: Measure the length and the breadth of the floor with a measuring tape, in metres.
Area of the floor = Length × Breadth, in square m. Perimeter = 2 × Length + 2 × Breadth, in metres.
Sample answer with practice values: a floor 8 m long and 6 m broad.
Area: 8 × 6 = 48 square m.
Perimeter: 2 × 8 = 16 and 2 × 6 = 12, and 16 + 12 = 28 m.
Check: 8 + 6 + 8 + 6 = 28. Your answer may differ, because your classroom may be a different size.
content.answer: Sample answer with practice values: 8 m by 6 m gives an area of 48 square m and a perimeter of 28 m. Your answer may differ.

(e): 6 cm by 5 cm. Area: 6 × 5 = 30 square cm. Perimeter: 6 + 5 + 6 + 5 = 22 cm.
Check: (a) and (d) are squares, so their length and breadth are equal.

content.question: Preetha and Adrit's grandmother is making another square patchwork. She arranges the patches as shown below. Can you guess how many patches she will need? How did you find it?
steps: We do not need to count the patches one by one. Look at the rows.
There are 6 rows, and each row has 4 patches.
6 × 4 = 24, so she will need 24 patches.
The length of one side is 6 and the other side is 4, so Area = Length × Breadth = 6 cm × 4 cm = 24 square cm.
Check by columns: 4 columns of 6 patches, 4 × 6 = 24.
content.answer: 24 patches. Area = Length × Breadth = 6 cm × 4 cm = 24 square cm.
content.text:
1. We do not need to count the patches one by one. Look at the rows.
2. There are $6$ rows, and each row has $4$ patches.
3. $6 \times 4 = 24$, so she will need $24$ patches.
4. The length of one side is $6$ and the other side is $4$, so Area $=$ Length $\times$ Breadth $= 6\text{ cm} \times 4\text{ cm} = 24\text{ square cm}$.
5. Check by columns: $4$ columns of $6$ patches, $4 \times 6 = 24$.
Answer: $24$ patches. Area $=$ Length $\times$ Breadth $= 6\text{ cm} \times 4\text{ cm} = 24\text{ square cm}$.

content.question: All the sides of a rectangle are equal, that is, the case of a square. Think about a square whose sides are 5 units long. What are its area and its perimeter?
steps: All the sides of a square are equal, so the length and the breadth are both 5 units.
Area of a square = Length × Length = 5 × 5 = 25 square cm.
Perimeter of a square = Length + Length + Length + Length = 4 × Length.
4 × 5 = 20, so the perimeter is 20 cm.
Check: adding the four sides, 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 20.
content.answer: Area = 5 × 5 = 25 square cm. Perimeter = 4 × 5 = 20 cm.

Answer: Area $= 5 \times 5 = 25\text{ square cm}$. Perimeter $= 4 \times 5 = 20\text{ cm}$.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a rectangular lawn has an area of 72 square m and a length of 9 m. How can you find its breadth?
2. We know that the area is length × breadth. So 9 times the breadth must be 72: some number times 9 makes 72.
3. To find that number, divide the area by the length: breadth = area ÷ length.
4. Check the answer by multiplying back: length × breadth must give the area.
5. Rule: breadth = area ÷ length, and length = area ÷ breadth.

content.text:
Worked example: A rectangular lawn has an area of 72 square m and a length of 9 m. What is its breadth?
1. Area = Length × Breadth, so 9 times the breadth is 72.
2. Find the breadth by dividing the area by the length: 72 ÷ 9 = 8.
3. Check by multiplying back: 9 × 8 = 72, which is the area.
4. The breadth is 8 m.
Answer: The breadth is 8 m

content.text:
1. Predict first: the height of a rectangle is marked in two parts, 5 cm and 7 cm. What is the whole height?
2. The two parts together make the whole side, so add them: 5 + 7 = 12 cm.
3. Then use the area rule with the whole sides: area = length × breadth.
4. You can check by finding the area of each part and adding: the parts of the area add up to the whole area.
5. Rule: when a side is marked in parts, add the parts to get the whole side, then multiply.

content.text:
Worked example: A rectangle is 20 cm wide. Its height is marked in two parts, 5 cm and 7 cm. Find the area of the rectangle.
1. The whole height is the two parts added: 5 + 7 = 12 cm.
2. Area = Length × Breadth = 20 × 12 = 240 square cm.
3. Check by parts: the upper part has an area of 20 × 5 = 100 and the lower part has an area of 20 × 7 = 140.
4. 100 + 140 = 240, the same area.
Answer: The area is 240 square cm

When a side is marked in parts, add the parts first.

media.teaching_notes: Predict first: a rectangular lawn has an area of 72 square m and a length of 9 m. How can you find its breadth? We know that the area is length × breadth. So 9 times the breadth must be 72: some number times 9 makes 72. To find that number, divide the area by the length: breadth = area ÷ length. Check the answer by multiplying back: length × breadth must give the area. Rule: breadth = area ÷ length, and length = area ÷ breadth. 1. Area = Length × Breadth, so 9 times the breadth is 72. 2. Find the breadth by dividing the area by the length: 72 ÷ 9 = 8. 3. Check by multiplying back: 9 × 8 = 72, which is the area. 4. The breadth is 8 m. Answer: The breadth is 8 m

Rule: when a side is marked in parts, add the parts to get the whole side, then multiply. 1. The whole height is the two parts added: 5 + 7 = 12 cm. 2. content.book_number: Let Us Do (using the rules), Q3
content.question: Find the area and perimeter of the following objects. Use a scale or measuring tape to find the length and the breadth of each of the objects. Objects: Cover of the Notebook; Newspaper; Blackboard; Ludo board; and two more objects of your own choice.
steps: For each object measure the length and the breadth with a scale or a measuring tape. Small objects are measured in centimetres and big ones in metres.
Area = Length × Breadth, in square cm or square m. Perimeter = 2 × Length + 2 × Breadth, in centimetres or metres.
Sample answer with practice values. Notebook cover, 24 cm by 18 cm: area 24 × 18 = 432 square cm; perimeter 2 × 24 = 48, 2 × 18 = 36 and 48 + 36 = 84 cm.
Newspaper, 60 cm by 40 cm: area 60 × 40 = 2400 square cm; perimeter 2 × 60 = 120, 2 × 40 = 80 and 120 + 80 = 200 cm.
Blackboard, 3 m by 1 m: area 3 × 1 = 3 square m; perimeter 2 × 3 = 6, 2 × 1 = 2 and 6 + 2 = 8 m.
Ludo board, 40 cm by 40 cm, a square: area 40 × 40 = 1600 square cm; perimeter 4 × 40 = 160 cm.
Rows 5 and 6: choose two objects of your own and do the same.
Check each perimeter by adding the four sides, for example 24 + 18 + 24 + 18 = 84. Your answer may differ.

content.question: Find the area of a rectangular field whose length is 42 m and breadth is 34 m.
steps: The area of a rectangle is Length × Breadth.
The length is 42 m and the breadth is 34 m, so the area is 42 × 34.
The area of the field is 1428 square m.
content.answer: 1428 square m
content.text:
1. The area of a rectangle is Length $\times$ Breadth.
2. The length is $42\text{ m}$ and the breadth is $34\text{ m}$, so the area is $42 \times 34$.
3. $42 \times 30 = 1260$.
4. $42 \times 4 = 168$.
5. $1260 + 168 = 1428$.
6. The area of the field is $1428\text{ square m}$.
7. Check: $34 \times 40 = 1360$ and $34 \times 2 = 68$, and $1360 + 68 = 1428$.
Answer: $1428\text{ square m}$

concepts.concept_name: Counting the Outer Edges of Tiles

content.text:
Take some square tiles and a die and play the game in pairs.
Do not move the tiles. The second player can take turn and add tiles to the same tiled figure.

content.text:
1. Predict first: two square tiles are joined along one edge, and each tile side is 1. How many outer edges does the figure have?
2. Every side of a tile is 1 unit long. The perimeter of a figure of tiles is the number of outer edges, the edges that are not shared with another tile.
3. Two tiles have 4 + 4 = 8 edges in all. The 2 edges where they touch are inside, so there are 8 − 2 = 6 outer edges and the perimeter is 6.
4. When you add a tile that touches the figure along 1 edge, the perimeter becomes 2 more. When the tile sits in a corner and touches 2 edges, the perimeter stays the same.
5. Rule: the perimeter of a figure of tiles is the number of its outer edges.

content.text:
Worked example: Five square tiles are placed like the letter L: 3 tiles in the top row and 2 more tiles below the left tile. Each tile side is 1. Find the perimeter. Then say what happens when one more tile is added at the end of the top row, and when one is added in the corner where the two arms meet.
1. Count the outer edges of each tile. The left tile of the top row has 2 outer edges, the middle tile 2 and the right tile 3.
2. Of the two lower tiles, the upper one has 2 outer edges and the lowest has 3.
3. Add: 2 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 12. The perimeter is 12.
4. A tile added at the end of the top row touches the figure along 1 edge, so the perimeter becomes 2 more: 12 + 2 = 14.
5. A tile added in the corner where the arms meet touches 2 edges, so the perimeter stays 12.
6. Check: counting the outer edges again, one by one, gives 12.
Answer: The perimeter is 12; one more tile at the end makes it 14, and one in the corner leaves it 12

content.text:
The perimeter of tiles is the number of outer edges.
A tile along 1 edge adds 2; a tile in a corner touching 2 edges adds nothing.
The player who makes the perimeter exactly 24 wins.

media.title: Perimeter 24 Game

tool_config.title: Perimeter 24 Game
tool_config.idea: Find the perimeter of a figure of square tiles by counting its outer edges, see how a tile added along one edge or in a corner changes it, and play the book's game to make the perimeter exactly 24.
tool_config.screen: Grandmother's floor, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. Square tiles lie on a mat in a pile and the figure that the players are building is the largest thing on screen, in the middle of the mat; every tile side is 1. A big die sits at the side. Every outer edge of the figure is marked 1 as in your maths book, and the marks light up as they are counted. Two player tags, Player 1 and Player 2, show whose turn it is, with an option to play against the tool instead of a friend. A banner says Make the perimeter 24. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: a Roll button that rolls the die from 1 to 6 and sets that number of tiles ready; drag the tiles of this turn so that they touch the figure along whole edges, and a tile cannot be moved once it is placed; a Count the edges button that lights each outer edge in turn; an Undo this turn button that takes back the tiles of this turn only; a Next player button; Check, Hint, Retry (undoes this turn), Reset (clears the figure), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the die number, the tiles placed, the perimeter counter (for example 12), the distance to 24 (for example 12 more), and a card number out of 7.
student_does: Look at a figure of 3 tiles in a row (practice values) with its outer edges marked 1. Count the outer edges one by one and say what number you get. That number is the perimeter.
Roll and place tiles in two different shapes and count the perimeters, add one tile along one edge, add one tile in a corner, and play to a perimeter of 16.

Play the book's game: find the perimeter of the tiles, add tiles to the same figure without moving any tile, and take turns till the perimeter becomes 24. The one who makes the perimeter 24 wins the game.
challenges: Card 1 (practice values): the die shows 4. Place the 4 tiles in a row and count the perimeter, then place them as a square of 2 by 2 and count again. Answer: a row of 4 has 4 + 1 + 4 + 1 = 10 outer edges, and a 2 by 2 square has 8. The same number of tiles can have different perimeters.

Card 2 (practice values): start with the 2 by 2 square, perimeter 8. Add 1 tile that touches the square along 1 edge. What is the perimeter now? Answer: 10, because 8 + 2 = 10. A tile along 1 edge makes the perimeter 2 more.

Card 3 (practice values): start with 3 tiles placed like the letter L, perimeter 8. Add 1 tile in the corner where the two arms meet. What is the perimeter now? Answer: 8. The tile touches 2 edges, so the perimeter stays the same, and the figure becomes a 2 by 2 square.

Card 4 (practice values): make a figure with a perimeter of exactly 16. Answer: any figure with 16 outer edges is right, for example a row of 7 tiles, because 7 + 1 + 7 + 1 = 16. Your figure may differ.
Challenge: 'Find the perimeter of the tiles.' The figure has 4 tiles: a row of 3 and one tile below the left tile. Answer: the perimeter is 10, because the outer edges are 3 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 10.

Challenge: 'Do not move the tiles. The second player can take turn and add tiles to the same tiled figure.' The die shows 1. Add 1 tile along 1 edge of the figure of 4 tiles. Answer: the figure has 5 tiles and the perimeter is 12, because 10 + 2 = 12.

Challenge: 'Take turns and add tiles to the same figure till the perimeter becomes 24. The one who makes the perimeter 24 wins the game.' The die shows 6. Add 6 tiles to the figure of 5 tiles without moving any tile. Answer: the figure has 11 tiles and the perimeter is 24, so the player who rolled the 6 wins. Another game may go differently.
feedback: The perimeter counter changes each time a tile is placed, and the tool says for example: This figure has 12 outer edges, so its perimeter is 12.
Count the edges lights each outer edge in turn and the counter goes up by one for each, so the student can check the total.

A tile that touches the figure along 1 edge makes the tool say: This tile touches 1 edge, so the perimeter is 2 more. A tile in a corner that touches 2 edges makes it say: This tile touches 2 edges, so the perimeter stays the same.
A tile that does not touch the figure along a whole edge slides back softly and the tool says: Place the tile so that it touches the figure along a whole edge.

When the perimeter goes past 24 the tool says: Past 24. A tile that fills a notch and touches 3 edges makes it 2 less. It never shows a red cross; the banner lights up and the player wins when the counter shows exactly 24.
tool_config.done_when: The student has counted the perimeter of figures of tiles by their outer edges, has seen what a tile along one edge and a tile in a corner do to the perimeter, has made a perimeter of 16, and has played the book's game to a perimeter of exactly 24.

To reach 24 from a perimeter of 12, you need 12 more. The tool places a tile along 1 edge so you can see the perimeter become 14.

content.question: Find the perimeter of the tiles.
steps: Each side of a tile is 1. The perimeter is the number of outer edges.
Count along the top: the 3 tiles of the top row show 3 outer edges.
Count down the right side of the top row: 1 outer edge.
Count under the top row, along the two tiles on the right: 2 outer edges.
Count the edge on the right of the lower tile and the edge under it: 1 + 1 = 2 outer edges.
Count the left side of both tiles: 2 outer edges.
Add: 3 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 10. The perimeter of the tiles is 10.

content.text:
1. Each side of a tile is $1$. The perimeter is the number of outer edges.
2. Count along the top: the $3$ tiles of the top row show $3$ outer edges.
3. Count down the right side of the top row: $1$ outer edge.
4. Count under the top row, along the two tiles on the right: $2$ outer edges.
[Image: Let Us Play: Ans1: solution]
5. Count the edge on the right of the lower tile and the edge under it: $1 + 1 = 2$ outer edges.
6. Count the left side of both tiles: $2$ outer edges.
7. Add: $3 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 10$. The perimeter of the tiles is $10$.
8. Check: $4$ tiles have $4 \times 4 = 16$ edges in all, and the $3$ places where tiles touch hide $2$ edges each, $3 \times 2 = 6$, so $16 - 6 = 10$.
Answer: $10$

content.question: Take turns and add tiles to the same figure till the perimeter becomes 24. The one who makes the perimeter 24 wins the game.
steps: Start with the 4 tiles from before: the perimeter is 10.
Player 1 rolls a 1 and adds 1 tile that touches the figure along 1 edge. The perimeter becomes 2 more: 10 + 2 = 12, with 5 tiles.
Player 2 rolls a 6 and adds 6 tiles to the same figure, without moving any tile. The figure now has 11 tiles.
Count the edges of 11 tiles: 11 × 4 = 44.
10 places where tiles touch each hide 2 edges: 10 × 2 = 20.
The perimeter is 44 − 20 = 24.
Player 2 has made the perimeter exactly 24, so Player 2 wins. Your game may go differently. Your answer may differ.

content.text:
1. Predict first: you have walked through the whole patchwork room. Can you say one idea from each stop, from the quilt border to the tile game? Read the lines below and tick each idea you remembered.
2. Perimeter: the length of the whole border of a shape, found by adding all its sides. A quilt 15 patches long and 10 patches broad has a border of 15 + 10 + 15 + 10 = 50 units.
3. Check: a shape with 3 equal sides of 6 cm has a perimeter of 3 × 6 = 18 cm.
4. Tiles and area: tiles cover with no gaps and no overlaps. Squares, rectangles and triangles tile; circles leave gaps. The area is the number of tiles that cover the region, in the unit of the tile.
5. Check: 24 square tiles cover a tray. Cut each one into 2 triangles and 48 triangles cover the same tray, because 24 × 2 = 48.
6. Comparing and the unit square: if one shape fits inside the other it has the smaller area. If not, count unit squares on a grid. The area of a square with sides 1 cm is 1 square cm, and 2 half squares make 1 square.
7. Check: 7 × 2 = 14 and 4 × 4 = 16, so a 4 by 4 square has a larger area than a 7 by 2 rectangle.
8. Area and perimeter are different measures. Shapes with the same area can have different perimeters: 16 squares as 4 by 4, 8 by 2 and 16 by 1 have perimeters 16, 20 and 34.
9. Check: shapes with the same perimeter can have different areas. With a perimeter of 20 units, a 5 by 5 square has area 25 and a 9 by 1 strip has area 9.
10. Rectangle: area = length × breadth and perimeter = 2 × length + 2 × breadth. For 8 by 5: the area is 8 × 5 = 40 square cm and the perimeter is 8 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 26 cm.
11. Square: area = length × length and perimeter = 4 × length. For a side of 7 cm: the area is 7 × 7 = 49 square cm and the perimeter is 4 × 7 = 28 cm.
12. Missing side: breadth = area ÷ length. A lawn of area 72 square m and length 9 m has a breadth of 72 ÷ 9 = 8 m. When a side is marked in parts, add the parts first.
13. Tiles and the game: the perimeter of a figure of tiles is the number of its outer edges. A tile added along 1 edge makes the perimeter 2 more, and a tile in a corner touching 2 edges leaves it the same.
14. Check: 5 tiles placed like the letter L have a perimeter of 12, and one more tile at the end of the top row makes it 14.

objectives.objective_text: Students find the perimeter of a shape by adding the length of every side, and by multiplying when all the sides are equal.
Students find the length of lace that covers the border of the quilt and the perimeter of shapes whose sides are all equal.
Students name the shapes that cover a table top without gaps and overlaps and the shape that leaves gaps.
Students find the area of a region as the number of tiles that cover it and say it in the unit of the tile.
Students count the tiles on the rug, the tables and the desk and say the area in the unit of the tile.
Students compare two areas by laying one shape on the other when one fits inside, and by counting equal squares when it does not.
Students find the area of a shape on a square grid by counting unit squares, and count two half squares as one square.
Students compare the areas of rectangles and gardens by counting unit squares on a grid.
Students find the perimeters of shapes that have the same area and see that the perimeters can be different.
Students find the areas of shapes that have the same perimeter and see that a bigger area does not always mean a bigger perimeter.
Students find the area and the perimeter of the mats and shapes in the questions and say what they notice about them.
Students find the area of a rectangle by multiplying its length and its breadth, as the number of rows times the number of patches in a row.
Students find the perimeter of a rectangle by adding its four sides, and by 2 × length + 2 × breadth.
Students find the area and the perimeter of a square from the length of one side.
Students find the area and the perimeter of rectangles and squares, and draw rectangles with a given perimeter.
Students find the breadth of a rectangle from its area and its length by dividing.
Students find the area of a rectangle whose side is marked in two parts by adding the parts first.
Students find the area and perimeter of objects they measure, using the rules for area and perimeter, and the area of a field, a missing breadth and the area of a figure with a side marked in parts.
